items.title: MagicBeanStalk: Escaping the RLVR Zero Advantage Trap with Recursive Data Synthesis
items.summary: Data-centric scaling of RLVR often results in a "zero advantage trap" where large datasets do not provide useful learning signals. To generate effective data, synthetic problems must require the reasoning and composition skills needed to solve hard problems while being calibrated for success and failure within a training budget. MagicBeanStalk introduces a recursive data-synthesis algorithm to grow seed problems into new, policy- and budget-calibrated training problems. This method improves performance on benchmarks like gpt-oss-120b and DeepSeek v4Flash in math, and yields improvements in finance as well. The approach effectively synthesizes verifiable problems, leading to significant performance gains across different domains.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "MagicBeanStalk: Escaping the RLVR Zero Advantage Trap with Recursive Data Synthesis" reports on a new method for data-centric scaling in Reinforcement Learning from Vision and Reward, demonstrating a technique to overcome the zero advantage trap in large datasets. The research introduces a recursive data-synthesis algorithm designed to generate effective training data by ensuring synthetic problems require the necessary reasoning and composition skills while maintaining calibration for success and failure within a defined training budget. This method systematically grows seed problems into novel training problems. Empirical results indicate that this approach improves performance on benchmarks such as gpt-oss-120b and DeepSeek v4Flash in mathematical reasoning, alongside yielding performance improvements in finance. This approach effectively synthesizes verifiable problems, leading to significant performance gains across various domains. The advancement suggests a pathway toward more efficient and higher-quality data generation for complex AI systems.

items.title: Know What You Don't Know: Agentic Data Synthesis by Evolving Generation Space for Closed-Loop Learning
items.summary: The paper proposes EvoSyn, a learning-feedback-driven multi-agent framework for agentic data synthesis in closed-loop learning. It addresses the gap where observed weaknesses do not directly guide future data synthesis, by organizing synthesis around a revisable state specifying interaction factors. A role-specialized multi-agent system translates learner feedback into synthesis revisions, while a Designer sets directions and a Planner grounds them into executable experience. This process allows for adaptation to weak areas and expansion of the synthesis space by incorporating newly discovered factors. Experiments demonstrate that EvoSyn improves task success on benchmarks and yields higher-quality, broader synthetic experience.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "Know What You Don't Know: Agentic Data Synthesis by Evolving Generation Space for Closed-Loop Learning" details a multi-agent framework for agentic data synthesis in closed-loop learning that improves task success and yields higher-quality synthetic experience. The proposed method introduces EvoSyn, a learning-feedback-driven framework organized around a revisable state specifying interaction factors to address the limitation where observed weaknesses do not directly guide future data synthesis. This system employs a role-specialized multi-agent structure where learner feedback is translated into synthesis revisions by an agent system, while a Designer sets directions and a Planner grounds these revisions into executable experience, allowing adaptation to weak areas and expansion of the synthesis space through the incorporation of newly discovered factors. Experimental results confirm that EvoSyn increases task success on various benchmarks and generates synthetic experience of greater quality and breadth. This work suggests a pathway for more adaptive and efficient synthetic data generation in complex artificial intelligence systems.

items.title: SpireBench: Evaluating Long-Horizon Strategic Play of Agentic Models with Slay the Spire
items.summary: SpireBench evaluates the long-horizon strategic play of agentic models using the commercial deck-builder game Slay the Spire. The benchmark assesses how models make decisions over extended periods to determine long-term success. Frontier LLMs performed better than heuristic baselines and matched average human players initially, but their performance declined as the game extended. The study suggests that performance differences stem from how agents manage risk and utilize prior game knowledge effectively. SpireBench provides a comprehensive, long-horizon benchmark with tools to diagnose agent failures.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "SpireBench: Evaluating Long-Horizon Strategic Play of Agentic Models with Slay the Spire" details an evaluation of long-horizon strategic play by agentic models using the deck-builder game Slay the Spire. The study assessed how models make decisions over extended periods to determine long-term success in the game. Researchers conducted the evaluation using frontier large language models against heuristic baselines and average human players. Initial performance from the frontier models matched human players, but performance diminished as the game extended. The performance divergence was attributed to the agents' management of risk and the effective utilization of prior game knowledge. The benchmark offers a comprehensive tool for diagnosing agent failures in complex strategic environments. This research indicates the importance of risk management and knowledge retention for agentic systems operating over extended time horizons.

items.title: Beyond Binary Verifiable Rewards: Behavioral Self-Rewarding for SWE Agents
items.summary: Binary reward systems in reinforcement learning offer limited supervision for software engineering agents. Behavioral Self-Rewarding (BSR) is introduced as a method to refine rewards by allowing the policy to judge its own trajectories. BSR reuses the policy to compare debugging behaviors between different trajectories from the same task and verifier outcome. This process generates task-local scores that are converted into bounded auxiliary rewards, providing contrast without altering the pass/fail order. Experiments demonstrate that using these comparative judgments improves performance for SWE agents across evaluated models.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "Beyond Binary Verifiable Rewards: Behavioral Self-Rewarding for SWE Agents" details a method for refining rewards in software engineering agent training by employing Behavioral Self-Rewarding. This approach introduces a mechanism allowing the agent policy to judge its own trajectories to generate task-local scores that serve as bounded auxiliary rewards. The methodology involves reusing the policy to compare debugging behaviors across different trajectories from the same task and using a verifier outcome to establish these comparative judgments. These judgments are then converted into auxiliary rewards that provide contrast without changing the original pass or fail sequence. Experiments show that utilizing these comparative judgments improves the performance of software engineering agents across various evaluated models. This advancement suggests a pathway toward more nuanced supervision for complex agent tasks in the software engineering domain.

items.title: CLEAT: Learning Value-Guided Clarification for Interactive Agents
items.summary: The CLEAT framework addresses interactive intent alignment by learning value-guided clarification for agents dealing with incomplete information. It co-trains a clarification-value controller and a task policy using shared interaction outcomes. The method introduces a residual query value to quantify the task utility gained from asking a question instead of proceeding. This value is estimated through paired rollouts, training the controller to predict clarification value and the policy to select useful questions. CLEAT demonstrates significant performance gains across benchmarks by learning how to effectively use clarification in agent interactions.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "CLEAT: Learning Value-Guided Clarification for Interactive Agents" details a framework for interactive intent alignment that learns value-guided clarification for agents operating with incomplete information. The method co-trains a clarification-value controller and a task policy using shared interaction outcomes. The research introduces a residual query value to quantify the task utility gained from asking a question instead of proceeding, which is estimated through paired rollouts to train the controller to predict clarification value and the policy to select useful questions. CLEAT demonstrates significant performance gains across various benchmarks by learning how to effectively utilize clarification in agent interactions. This work indicates a method for improving agent decision-making in environments requiring clarification. Further research into value-guided interaction strategies is anticipated.

items.title: EliteTable: Self-Improving Program Search for Executable Control Policies
items.summary: EliteTable is a self-improving program-search algorithm that utilizes large language models to guide the search process. It employs a fixed-capacity table of high-scoring solutions to inform new proposals, edits, and remixes of existing solutions. Performance was tested across six Gymnasium control tasks, evaluating performance over ten generations. Results showed performance improvements for selected-winner searches and the transfer of gains to new episodes in some tasks. The work documents improvement during program search and the transfer of learned advantages to new environments.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "EliteTable: Self-Improving Program Search for Executable Control Policies" details a self-improving program-search algorithm that uses large language models to guide the search process, demonstrating performance improvements across various control tasks. The research introduced EliteTable, an algorithm that employs a fixed-capacity table of high-scoring solutions to inform subsequent proposals, edits, and remixes of those solutions. Performance was evaluated across six Gymnasium control tasks over ten generations, revealing performance improvements for selected-winner searches and the transfer of learned advantages to new episodes in certain tasks. This work documents the improvement achieved during program search and the successful transfer of learned advantages to new environments. This development indicates progress in autonomous program discovery and the ability of large language models to enhance complex control policy optimization.

items.title: Market Impact Estimation via Causal Foundation Models
items.summary: Market impact is a causal quantity, but classical models are biased because they regress price on flow, ignoring informational flow. A Causal Market Simulator, a causal prior-data fitted network, is proposed to address this by explicitly modeling the confounding informational flow. The model demonstrates that an intervention-ablated twin collapses to the pre-window mean, and the model successfully tracks true-parameter oracles in complex markets. Applying the model to actual flow bursts in various markets suggests causal transfer, with further refinement showing that impact accrues over execution duration.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.LG, "Market Impact Estimation via Causal Foundation Models" reports on a novel approach to estimating market impact. The research introduces a Causal Market Simulator, a causal prior-data fitted network designed to explicitly model the confounding informational flow in market dynamics. The model demonstrated that an intervention-ablated twin collapses to the pre-window mean, and the simulator successfully tracks true-parameter oracles in complex markets. Applying this framework to actual flow bursts across various markets suggests a causal transfer mechanism, with subsequent refinement indicating that market impact accrues over the duration of execution. This work advances the ability to model complex financial causality using foundation models. Further research will focus on deploying these causal structures in real-time trading environments.

items.title: Representation Alignment from a Few Paired Data via Distilled Optimal Transport
items.summary: The method aligns representations from few paired data points using distilled optimal transport. It achieves this by expressing representations based on similarities to the paired anchors, placing both modalities in a common coordinate system. A single entropic optimal transport problem is solved over the entire data pool to ensure the matching counteracts hubness. The resulting plan is then distilled into lightweight encoders, making the correspondence inductive. Evaluation on image-text and molecule-text alignment shows superior performance over existing methods.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "Representation Alignment from a Few Paired Data via Distilled Optimal Transport" details a method for aligning representations from limited paired data points using distilled optimal transport. The research demonstrates that the approach achieves alignment by expressing representations based on similarities to paired anchors and placing both modalities into a common coordinate system. A single entropic optimal transport problem is solved across the entire data pool to counteract hubness, and the resulting plan is distilled into lightweight encoders, making the correspondence inductive. Evaluation on image-text and molecule-text alignment shows superior performance compared to existing methods. This work indicates a pathway for more effective representation learning with sparse data. Future developments are expected to focus on scaling this distillation technique across larger datasets.

items.title: Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality
items.summary: Heavy-tailed spectral distributions in trained weight matrices are strongly predictive of deep neural network quality. This work investigates the statistical reasons behind this predictive success by using a probabilistic framework on final layer weights. The authors find that the limiting log-marginal likelihood for spectra following the High-Temperature Marchenko-Pastur distribution predicts model quality. They derive an optimal heaviness parameter that empirically predicts overfitting in large-scale DNNs. Ultimately, analyzing these heavy-tailed spectra offers a practical predictor of complex model performance.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - stat.ML, "Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" investigates the statistical reasons behind the predictive success of heavy-tailed weight spectra in deep neural networks. The study demonstrates that the limiting log-marginal likelihood for spectra following the High-Temperature Marchenko-Pastur distribution predicts model quality. The research employed a probabilistic framework on final layer weights to analyze the statistical underpinnings of this correlation. The authors derived an optimal heaviness parameter that empirically predicts overfitting in large-scale deep neural networks by analyzing these heavy-tailed spectra. Analyzing these specific weight distributions offers a practical predictor of complex model performance. This analysis provides a quantifiable statistical tool for assessing the quality and potential overfitting of large artificial intelligence models.

items.title: Faithfulness Without Anchors: A Position Paper on the Structural Misalignments of Explainable AI Faithfulness Metrics for Feature Importance
items.summary: Explainable AI tools often fail to increase trust and instead promote overreliance on incorrect predictions. This limitation stems from XAI methods oversimplifying model internals, causing a misalignment known as unfaithfulness. Faithfulness is the approximation between an explanation and the model, and rigorously computing it is crucial for quantifying explanation trustworthiness. Current faithfulness metrics suffer from significant limitations, making quantification of trustworthiness infeasible or computationally expensive. The paper outlines these shortcomings and proposes research avenues to improve the reliability of faithfulness metrics.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "Faithfulness Without Anchors: A Position Paper on the Structural Misalignments of Explainable AI Faithfulness Metrics for Feature Importance" details the structural misalignments in explainable artificial intelligence faithfulness metrics concerning feature importance. The research addresses the limitation where current XAI methods oversimplify model internals, leading to a misalignment termed unfaithfulness, which diminishes trust rather than increasing it. The paper examines the approximation between an explanation and the model, noting that rigorously computing faithfulness is essential for quantifying explanation trustworthiness. The authors outline the significant limitations present in existing faithfulness metrics, demonstrating that current methods render the quantification of trustworthiness either infeasible or computationally expensive. The work proposes new research avenues aimed at improving the reliability of these critical faithfulness metrics. This research indicates a need for more rigorous mathematical foundations in assessing the reliability of explanations in deployed AI systems.

items.title: GlucoPRISM: Protocol-Supervised Pretraining for Cross-Cohort Glucose Transfer
items.summary: GlucoPRISM uses protocol-supervised pretraining to facilitate cross-cohort glucose transfer in foundation models. It supervises a GlucoFM backbone with response contracts dictating how representation components should change when only day, sensor, or both are altered. Supervision is derived from synthetic sensor views calibrated on paired recordings and glucose summaries, without clinical labels. Removing the sensor band improved transfer AUROC, demonstrating that a device-related component hinders transfer. This method improved performance across multiple public tasks and clinical endpoints by effectively filtering out device-specific noise.

items.title: Faithful and Complete LLM-Assisted Automated Construction of Hierarchical Hardware Knowledge Graphs
items.summary: The research presents an automated pipeline using Large Language Models (LLMs) to construct hierarchical hardware knowledge graphs from hardware datasheets. This process involves chunk-based property extraction, hierarchical routing, and iterative refinement to manage the fragmented and heterogeneous information in datasheets. The framework leverages LLMs for extraction and reasoning while preserving source provenance and using validated instructions for graph updates. Evaluation shows the method achieves 98.8% property faithfulness compared to a one-shot baseline. These improvements yield more reliable and comprehensive engineering information for hardware design and verification.

items.title: Equal-Budget Monte Carlo Tree Search versus Randomized-Restart List Scheduling for DAG Workflows: A Controlled Equal-Budget Computational Study
items.summary: A controlled computational study compared Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) and randomized-restart list scheduling for Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) workflows with equal budgets. MCTS performed 2.88% worse than the restarts across 2048 evaluated schedules, though restarts showed self-improvement on a separate pool. The performance difference depended on the workflow structure, winning for restarts on sparse irregular workflows but showing no difference on regular layered ones. Swapping to textbook UCT scheduling reduced the deficit, confirming the context-dependent nature of the performance. The results were based on a controlled synthetic domain with limited task counts and processor numbers.

items.title: Kairos: Toward a Byte-Level Foundation Model for Every Modality
items.summary: Kairos proposes a byte-level foundation model capable of handling every modality by training on a shared one-byte space for text, image, audio, video, lidar, and control streams. It integrates bidirectional gated-DeltaNet linear attention, sliding-window attention, and a sparse Mixture-of-Experts feed-forward layer. The model utilizes a multi-scale byte-level codec and is trained with a uniform-noise denoising objective across these modalities. Sanity checks indicate that the proposed combination optimizes the implementation, with attention variants reaching a minimum loss near $10^{-3}$. The work suggests optimization but points to further multimodal training for generalization.

items.title: Efficient Learning of Survival Analysis Models Under Outcome-Dependent Truncation and Censoring
items.summary: The research addresses the efficient learning of survival analysis models when data involves outcome-dependent truncation and censoring. The work connects the fields of learning under truncation and survival analysis, addressing limitations in existing methods that rely on iterative procedures. It demonstrates that Cox regression can be efficiently learned using first-order optimization when the baseline hazard is known, even with nonconvexity. When the baseline hazard is learned jointly, the method constructs identifiable models with correctly specified negative log-likelihoods. Experiments show that accounting for truncation reduces prediction bias in both Cox regression and neural networks, with significant speedups over expectation maximization.

items.title: From Imbalance to Evidence: Deep Nonparametric Testing for Complex Data under Severe Sample Imbalance
items.summary: Severe sample imbalance challenges standard two-sample tests, especially for complex, non-Euclidean data like graphs. The research investigates how to utilize abundant majority observations to maintain sensitivity to smaller samples during distributional comparisons. A novel framework, the Enhanced Imbalance-Aware Deep Classifier Two-Sample Test (EIAD-C2ST), is proposed to address this issue. This method incorporates imbalance into the testing evidence rather than treating it as a nuisance for training. The study establishes theoretical guarantees and demonstrates empirical performance gains by leveraging majority-sample surplus as statistical evidence.

items.title: Scalable Learning of Determinantal Point Processes with Kernel-Structured Interactions
items.summary: Determinantal Point Processes (DPPs) use a kernel matrix to encode item similarities, but scaling their learning to large datasets requires structural constraints that limit expressive power. The study addresses this trade-off by modeling full-rank interactions using nonlinear kernels and latent features. A surrogate function for the maximum likelihood estimator and stochastic optimization with random features are employed for scalable learning. Numerical experiments show that this method achieves better generalization and parameter efficiency on real-world data.

items.title: Generalized Determinantal Point Processes for Attraction and Repulsion with Distinct Interaction Kernels
items.summary: Determinantal point processes (DPPs) model repulsion, but Nonsymmetric DPPs (NDPPs) capture both attraction and repulsion, although their kernels are hard to interpret. The determinant-ratio point process (DRPP) is proposed to model both attraction and repulsion through the ratio of two symmetric positive-definite kernels. This formulation preserves the feature-based interpretation of standard DPPs while allowing separate specification of the two effects. The DRPP framework naturally characterizes attraction structures, such as clustered attraction, with a rank directly related to the number of latent groups. Experimental results indicate that DRPPs are more parameter-efficient than NDPPs for fitting transitive attraction.

items.title: Sparse Dictionary Learning for Measure-Valued Data via Linearized Optimal Transport: Efficient Algorithms and Sample Complexity
items.summary: The research studies dictionary learning for measure-valued data by embedding measures into Hilbert spaces using optimal transport geometry. It learns data-adapted dictionaries through sparse autoencoder parameterizations to create fast and scalable representations of probability measures as sparse codes. The framework merges the geometric structure of optimal transport with the efficiency of sparse representation learning across modalities like images and text embeddings. The authors prove generalization bounds for sparse dictionary learning objectives based on the metric complexity of the atom class. Finally, they derive explicit covering number bounds for optimal transport dictionaries, supporting a scalable representation learning model.

items.title: Two-way Guidance: Simultaneous Learning of Summary Statistics for Generative Bayes
items.summary: Bayesian simulation-based inference methods often struggle with recovering concentrated posteriors as observation size increases. The research proposes jointly learning sufficient summary statistics along with the posterior for scalable inference in various SBI methods. A key concept introduced is "two-way guidance," where structural restrictions on the summary simplify posterior learning, and a posterior objective guides the summary toward sufficiency. This mechanism explains why structural restrictions on summary statistics improve posterior learning performance. The work establishes theoretical guarantees on estimation error and summary sufficiency, defining conditions for recovering concentrated posteriors.

items.title: Universal Bounds for Self-Normalized Kullback-Leibler Estimation
items.summary: The work studies an entropy-based estimator for Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence derived from normalized importance weights. It establishes a universal finite-sample bound showing that the expectation of this estimator can exceed the target-proposal KL divergence by at most $\log 2$. The KL divergence between the importance-weighted resampling distribution and the proposal is bounded by both the estimator's expectation and the target KL divergence. Crucially, these bounds hold without requiring bounded importance weights or finite higher moments. The results are applicable to test-time alignment in generative models and relative entropy coding.

items.title: Beyond Second-Order Information: Paid Logistic Regression with Noisy Features
items.summary: The research focuses on online binary prediction using paid stochastic features where learners can spend resources for better feature observations. This is motivated by applications like medical testing, where cost yields more precise measurements. The study contrasts with previous results by showing that covariance information alone is insufficient for optimal logistic losses. Under a structural ordering of payments, the regret achieved is $\widetilde O(\sqrt{T})$ if the noise structure is known, and $\widetilde O(T^{2/3})$ if it is unknown. The work establishes lower bounds matching these regret rates.

items.title: CircuitTree: Composing Circuits into A Syllable Transcriber
items.summary: The work proposes CircuitTree, a method for composing multiple neural network circuits into a single model. It utilizes a greedy, density-scaled composition algorithm, generalized via CircuitTree, built on a $\Theta(N\log N)$ tree-compose schedule. The approach composes circuits pruned from HuBERT for phoneme classification into a syllable classifier. Chaining these CircuitTrees results in syllable transcription with 64.8\% accuracy. The method achieves this by sharing 99.5\% of circuit components across the components.

items.title: Fast Gradient-Based Approximation of Continuous Dynamic Time Warping
items.summary: Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) is slow and non-differentiable, leading to the proposal of Continuous-DTW (CDTW) with continuous warping functions. This paper introduces FastCDTW, an efficient approximate solver for CDTW with two strategies: an exact scheme for piecewise-linear functions and a Monte Carlo estimator for smooth functions like those from implicit neural networks. FastCDTW provides gradients necessary for optimization with respect to the warping function and input time series. The resulting algorithm is GPU-friendly and beneficial for complex machine learning tasks. This method is demonstrated in applications such as time series averaging and domain adaptation.

items.title: Algebraic Integer Quantization for Machine Learning Applications
items.summary: Algebraic integer number formats (AINF) provide a framework for highly configurable and accurate compressed computation by reducing calculations to purely integer arithmetic. This property allows for error-free multiply-accumulate operations, enabling a matrix multiplication engine with competitive performance on hardware accelerators. Algebraic integer quantization (AIQ) is a lossy compression format for large language model inference that optimizes based on specific numerical characteristics. Experiments show AIQ achieves accuracy comparable to the industry-standard MX format for LLM inference at equivalent bit-per-parameter budgets. Future work involves generalizing these concepts to higher-order and multidimensional algebraic integers.

items.title: Scan-Parallel Variational Inference for event-driven Latent Jump Models
items.summary: Latent jump models (LJMs) are introduced to model time series where the state undergoes deterministic evolution punctuated by Poisson-driven, state-dependent jumps. To train these models efficiently, Scan-Parallel Variational Inference (SPVI) is proposed, which samples the latent event configuration before evaluating the state recurrence. SPVI uses triangular affine scans to enable fast and scalable training for these jump models in logarithmic temporal depth. LJMs prove competitive with continuous-time models in forecast accuracy and are significantly faster to train than sequential baselines. This method allows modeling uncertain, unobserved shocks in systems that are not necessarily smooth or diffusive.

items.title: Enriched Holomorphic Neural Networks for 2D and 3D Laplace Problems
items.summary: Enriched holomorphic neural networks are combined with singular functions derived from local geometry to address singular behavior in 2D and 3D Laplace problems. This combination results in a harmonic representation that fits the smooth remainder from boundary data while capturing the singular behavior through enrichment terms. The singular exponents used in the construction are trainable, allowing the method to apply even when the local expansion is unknown. Extending the approach to three dimensions involves evaluating independent networks along complex null directions. The enriched model demonstrates superior accuracy, achieving margins several orders of magnitude better than other methods on radiation detector data.

items.title: Behind-the-Meter Photovoltaic Visibility from Net Smart Meters: Deployment Regimes and Operational Insights
items.summary: Distribution operators need behind-the-meter photovoltaic (PV) generation visibility, which can be achieved using deep-learning-based PV disaggregation from net smart meter data. The operational value of this disaggregation depends on deployment regimes that separate household transfer from temporal extrapolation. Benchmarking showed that the deployment regime explains more error variation than the model choice under fixed training conditions. Furthermore, fine-tuning on target-region households significantly reduces source-model transfer error. These results suggest using regime-matched error budgets and context-dependent selection for energy data analytics.

items.title: CacheScope: Exact-Compute Allocation for Training-Free Diffusion Acceleration
items.summary: CacheScope accelerates training-free diffusion inference by caching approximations instead of full denoising at specific steps. It addresses the issue where feature reuse leads to limited gains when reconstruction complexity increases. The method normalizes probe-output variation with input displacement to estimate a directional gain per unit trajectory movement. CacheScope selectively falls back to full denoising only when high-risk reuse steps are identified, without requiring additional training. This approach achieves up to 3.57x acceleration and a 70.1% reduction in LPIPS across several diffusion models.

items.title: An Input-Dependent Readout Phase for Resonant Sequence Models
items.summary: Resonant Sequence Models use a fixed-size state to avoid attention costs but require a design choice for state transitions. Modifying the readout phase to be input-dependent introduces content-dependent memory while retaining an exact convolutional path. This modification for ResonatorLM adjusts the readout phase based on the current token, adding input dependence. For character-level models on WikiText-2, this input-dependent phase matched the original at training length and improved performance upon extrapolation. The learned phase tracks the current character rather than distance, and the method removes failure beyond the training length.
